title: The Client Transfer Test: What Actually Decides What a Law or Accounting Practice Is Worth
linkedin:
Two accounting or law practices can report almost identical billings and still sell for very different prices.

The gap almost always comes down to one thing: what happens to the clients when the usual partner steps back.

In our experience, practices spend years watching utilisation and realisation rates, because those numbers drive this year's profit. Fair enough. But a buyer is not paying for this year's fee base. They are paying for next year's, under someone else's name.

That is a different question entirely, and it explains why a firm with a strong senior partner and a thinner layer underneath often prices lower than the P&L would suggest.

The practices that see their fee multiple and eventual sale price land close together are the ones that treat client transfer as a multi-year project. Introducing a second person into key files. Letting them lead the smaller matters first. Gradually shifting who the client calls first.

Started six months before a retirement or sale, this rarely holds. Started two to three years out, it usually does.

If you are a partner or principal thinking a few years ahead, the fee base was never the whole story. The transfer question is.

facebook:
Quick one for any accountants, bookkeepers or lawyers reading this: if you had to step back from your practice tomorrow, would your best clients stay, or would they follow you out the door?

It is not a trick question. Most owner-led practices have never actually tested it, because the day to day billings look fine either way.

But it is usually the single biggest thing that decides what a practice is worth when a partner retires or a sale comes up. Not the fee base. Whether the relationships transfer.

Worth thinking about well before you need the answer.

A note for accounting and law practice owners across Queensland and the East Coast, especially if a partner's retirement or a sale is somewhere on the horizon, even a distant one.

Most practices measure their value using a fairly standard rule of thumb, a multiple of fees or maintainable earnings. That is a reasonable starting point, but it misses the question that actually decides the final number: when a client's usual partner steps back, does that client stay with the practice, or does the relationship go with the person.

We see this gap most often in practices with a strong senior partner and a thinner layer underneath. The billings look healthy every year. What is less visible is how much of that fee base depends on one person's personal relationships rather than something the whole practice can carry forward.

The good news is that this is fixable, but it takes time. Genuinely transferring a client relationship, introducing a second person, letting them take the lead on smaller matters, tends to take two to three years done properly, not the final months before a sale.

If succession or an eventual sale is on your mind, it is worth starting that conversation earlier than feels necessary.
